provenance.task: Does the way pain works reveal that all parts of an organism contribute to memory? + phantom limb pain (where we assume the brain is doing it)

findings.claim: Pain trace held non-cortically (nociceptor CPEB = F248 molecule, DRG, spinal central sensitization Woolf 1983, C-fibre LTP, glia, methylation). Phantom limb pain contested: DRG lidocaine extinguishes it (Vaso/Devor 2014); Makin 2018 finds PRESERVED cortex.
findings.citation: Bogen+Levine 2012 FETCHED; Woolf 1983 Nature 306:686 FETCHED; Sandkuhler 2007 FETCHED; Ji 2013 FETCHED; Vaso+Devor 2014 PMID24769187; Kikkert+Makin 2018 Cortex 106:174 FETCHED; Melzack 1990 PMID1691874.

opus_survey.cross_cutting: Pain memory is distributed across non-privileged levels (F248 shape); phantom = stored limb-attractor read after render removed, like planarian memory outliving the brain (F251). Lens fenced; no level privileged.
opus_survey.uncentered_note: Held all levels and both phantom poles without ranking; lens fenced.
gaps: F251 has no file (only F248/F249); some cites via secondary indices.

findings.item: PERIPHERAL SENSITIZATION — nociceptor and DRG hyperexcitability as a peripheral pain-memory trace
findings.claim: After tissue injury or nerve injury, primary sensory neurons (nociceptors) whose cell bodies reside in the dorsal root ganglion (DRG) enter a persistent state of lowered firing threshold, increased spontaneous activity, and altered gene expression. This constitutes a memory-like trace held in peripheral tissue — below and independent of the brain. The trace is maintained by altered ion-channel expression (Nav1.7/1.8/1.9 upregulation, potassium channel downregulation), transcriptional reprogramming, and interactions with satellite glial cells (SGCs) and immune cells. The DRG has been shown to be a more robust source of spontaneous ectopic firing than stump neuromas in head-to-head comparisons. Walters (2012) demonstrated that after spinal cord injury, uninjured nociceptors enter a 'persistent hyperfunctional state' that persists even when dissociated DRG neurons are placed in low-density culture without serum or growth factors — showing the trace is intrinsic to the cell, not dependent on continued external signaling. Berta, Qadri, Tan, and Ji (2017) document 'major cellular and molecular changes' in DRG including phenotypic switching (touch-sensitive mechanoreceptors acquiring pain-transmission capacity) as persistent pain substrates.
findings.citation: Walters ET. 'Nociceptors as chronic drivers of pain and hyperreflexia after spinal cord injury: an adaptive-maladaptive hyperfunctional state hypothesis.' Frontiers in Physiology 2012, 3:309. DOI: 10.3389/fphys.2012.00309. Open access PMC3429080. | Berta T, Qadri Y, Tan PH, Ji RR. 'Targeting dorsal root ganglia and primary sensory neurons for the treatment of chronic pain.' Expert Opinion on Therapeutic Targets 2017. DOI: 10.1080/14728222.2017.1328057. PMC5890331.

findings.item: SATELLITE GLIAL CELLS (SGCs) in DRG as non-neuronal peripheral pain memory
findings.claim: SGCs envelop DRG neuron somata and respond to injury and inflammation by upregulating GFAP, increasing gap junction (connexin-43) coupling, releasing CXCL1, and depressing Kir4.1 channels — all of which sustain neuronal hyperexcitability at the ganglionic level. Du et al. (2023) showed that carrageenan injection triggers SGC activation in DRG, with activated SGCs secreting CXCL1 which activates PKCe in sensory neurons — a key molecular marker of the acute-to-chronic pain transition (hyperalgesic priming). Blocking CXCL1 prevented PKCe overproduction and reduced hyperalgesia. This constitutes a non-neuronal (glial) peripheral memory mechanism at the level of the DRG, below the spinal cord. Note: SGC involvement in DRG is distinct from spinal microglia/astrocytes; this is peripheral glial memory.
findings.citation: Du J, Yi M, Xi D, Wang S, Liu B, Shao X, Liang Y, He X, Fang J, Fang J. 'Satellite glial cells drive the transition from acute to chronic pain in a rat model of hyperalgesic priming.' Frontiers in Molecular Neuroscience 2023, 16:1089162. DOI: 10.3389/fnmol.2023.1089162. Open access.

findings.item: SPINAL CENTRAL SENSITIZATION — Woolf's original 1983 demonstration; the spinal cord holds a pain memory trace BELOW the brain
findings.claim: Clifford Woolf published the foundational central sensitization finding in Nature in 1983: after peripheral injury in an animal model, the spinal cord's flexor reflex threshold dropped persistently, and the injury-induced increase in excitability arose in part from changes in spinal cord activity — not only from peripheral changes. This was the first demonstration that the spinal cord, not merely the periphery or the brain, holds a persistent change in nociceptive gain after injury. The term 'central sensitization' was coined here to name a spinal-cord-level plasticity. Critically, this sensitization renders previously non-painful stimuli painful and expands the body-surface area that generates pain — both features resembling memory-like generalization of a pain state.
findings.citation: Woolf CJ. 'Evidence for a central component of post-injury pain hypersensitivity.' Nature 1983, 306:686-688. DOI: 10.1038/306686a0. PubMed PMID: 6656869. [Open access abstract; full text paywalled — citation verified via PubMed and Semantic Scholar.]

findings.item: SPINAL CENTRAL SENSITIZATION — Woolf and Latremoliere 2009 comprehensive mechanistic account
findings.claim: Latremoliere and Woolf (2009) provide a comprehensive mechanistic account of central sensitization as 'increases in membrane excitability and synaptic efficacy as well as reduced inhibition' in spinal dorsal horn neurons. They make the critical point that once central sensitization is established, 'pain is no longer coupled to the presence, intensity, or duration of noxious peripheral stimuli.' This is a memory-like feature: the trace persists after the initial drive is removed. The mechanisms are principally spinal: NMDA receptor activation, AMPA receptor trafficking, removal of Mg2+ block, increased BDNF signaling, loss of inhibitory interneuron function — all at the dorsal horn level.
findings.citation: Latremoliere A and Woolf CJ. 'Central sensitization: a generator of pain hypersensitivity by central neural plasticity.' The Journal of Pain 2009. DOI: 10.1016/j.jpain.2009.06.012. PubMed PMID: 19712899.

findings.item: SPINAL CENTRAL SENSITIZATION — Woolf 2011 consensus framing
findings.claim: Woolf's 2011 PAIN review cements central sensitization as the canonical spinal-pain-memory concept: nociceptor inputs trigger a 'prolonged but reversible increase in the excitability and synaptic efficacy of neurons in central nociceptive pathways,' manifesting as allodynia, secondary hyperalgesia, and enhanced temporal summation. The location is explicitly central nervous system but primarily spinal: dorsal horn neurons are the substrate, with downstream thalamic and cortical effects secondary to the spinal state change.
findings.citation: Woolf CJ. 'Central sensitization: Implications for the diagnosis and treatment of pain.' PAIN 2011, 152(3 Suppl):S2-S15. DOI: 10.1016/j.pain.2010.09.030. [Verified via multiple independent citation databases.]

findings.item: SPINAL WIND-UP and LTP — Ji, Kohno, Moore, Woolf 2003 explicit 'pain and memory' framing
findings.claim: Ji, Kohno, Moore, and Woolf (2003) in Trends in Neurosciences explicitly ask whether pain and memory share similar mechanisms, comparing spinal central sensitization to hippocampal LTP. They note that central sensitization 'bears a striking resemblance to LTP, an NMDA-mediated process believed to be the neurobiological basis for learning and memory,' and that 'lasting pain states are in essence a nociceptive memory.' This is mainstream pain neuroscience explicitly treating spinal sensitization as a memory-class phenomenon — and locating the key substrate in the SPINAL cord, not the brain. Wind-up (progressive increase in dorsal horn action potential firing during repeated C-fiber stimulation) is the temporal summation phenomenon that can trigger this LTP-like change.
findings.citation: Ji RR, Kohno T, Moore KA, Woolf CJ. 'Central sensitization and LTP: do pain and memory share similar mechanisms?' Trends in Neurosciences 2003, 26(12):696-705. DOI: 10.1016/j.tins.2003.09.017. PubMed PMID: 14624855.

findings.item: SPINAL LTP — Sandkuhler 2007 review of LTP specifically in spinal nociceptive pathways
findings.claim: Sandkuhler (2007) reviews spinal LTP as a distinct form of synaptic plasticity at C-fiber synapses onto lamina I NK1-expressing neurons in the dorsal horn. LTP here is inducible by 'natural, low or high frequency, asynchronous and irregular discharge patterns in sensory nerve fibres' — unlike hippocampal LTP which requires synchronized high-frequency input. Sandkuhler notes hippocampal LTP is the prime model for learning and memory, and that spinal LTP involves 'the same essential elements' as hyperalgesia. However, he does not explicitly claim the spinal cord holds memory independent of the brain — the focus is on local spinal amplification within pain pathways, with the state change potentially subject to descending modulation. [Honest flag: the spinal-LTP-as-independent-memory claim is a framework reading; the primary literature says LTP-like plasticity holds at spinal synapses and contributes to pain persistence, not that the spinal cord is an autonomous memory organ.] Ruscheweyh et al. (2011) extend this: spinal LTP as a target for pain therapy, with two intervention strategies — prevention of LTP formation, or reversal of established LTP.
findings.citation: Sandkuhler J. 'Understanding LTP in pain pathways.' Molecular Pain 2007, 3:9. DOI: 10.1186/1744-8069-3-9. Open access PMC1852298. | Ruscheweyh R, Wilder-Smith O, Drdla R, Liu XG, Sandkuhler J. 'Long-term potentiation in spinal nociceptive pathways as a novel target for pain therapy.' Molecular Pain 2011, 7:20. DOI: 10.1186/1744-8069-7-20. PubMed PMID: 21443797.

findings.item: GLIAL / NEUROINFLAMMATORY pain memory — microglia and astrocytes in spinal cord
findings.claim: Ji, Nackley, Huh, Terrando, and Maixner (2018, Anesthesiology) conceptualize chronic pain as a 'neuroimmune condition' where central sensitization is driven by neuroinflammation. Key findings: (1) Microglia activation (peaking within 10 days) correlates with mechanical allodynia and drives the acute-to-chronic transition; (2) Astrocytes show MORE PERSISTENT involvement — through 'gliopathy' (pathological functional switch where connexin-43 transitions from gap-junction to hemichannel mode, making astrocytes 'leaky'), releasing cytokines and chemokines that sustain spinal sensitization; (3) 'Gliogenic LTP can travel long distances via cerebrospinal fluid' enabling widespread pain across multiple body sites from a single injury; (4) Critically: in males, spinal microglia regulate neuropathic pain via p38 phosphorylation, but in females T cells appear to replace microglia in this role — a fundamental non-neuronal, immune-based pain memory mechanism with sex dimorphism. This is a non-neuronal, glial-immune distributed memory at the spinal level.
findings.citation: Ji RR, Nackley A, Huh Y, Terrando N, Maixner W. 'Neuroinflammation and central sensitization in chronic and widespread pain.' Anesthesiology 2018. DOI: 10.1097/ALN.0000000000002130. Open access PMC6051899.

findings.item: IMMUNE system pain memory — non-neuronal cells (T cells, macrophages, mast cells) holding peripheral pain trace
findings.claim: Jain, Hakim, and Woolf (2024, Journal of Experimental Medicine) argue pain should be understood as a 'neuroimmune condition': macrophages produce IL-1beta, TNFalpha, IL-6 to drive peripheral sensitization; CD8+ T cells in DRG signal to macrophages via IL-13, promoting IL-10 release to resolve pain; regulatory T cells produce IL-35 to alleviate pain; mast cells, positioned close to nerve endings, release histamine, bradykinin, NGF, proteases on degranulation — causing immediate hyperalgesia. Mast cell-deficient mice show abrogated thermal and mechanical hyperalgesia. The sex dimorphism noted by Ji et al. (T cells replacing microglia in females) is confirmed here. This constitutes immune memory of a pain state — cells that are not neurons, distributed in peripheral tissue, maintaining hyperalgesia.
findings.citation: Jain A, Hakim S, Woolf CJ. 'Immune drivers of physiological and pathological pain.' Journal of Experimental Medicine 2024, 221(5):e20221687. DOI: 10.1084/jem.20221687. Open access PMC11010323.

findings.item: EPIGENETIC / molecular pain memory in DRG — DNA methylation reprogramming persisting weeks after nerve injury
findings.claim: Garriga, Laumet, Chen, Zhang, Madzo, Issa, Pan, and Jelinek (2018, Journal of Neuroscience) demonstrate that peripheral nerve injury causes widespread DNA hypomethylation in DRG. Key: changes detected at 3 DAYS post-injury remained detectable at 3 WEEKS — across the acute-to-chronic pain transition. Approximately 8% of CpG sites were altered, affecting 788 hypomethylated and 167 hypermethylated genes, with enrichment in nervous system development and cytokine-receptor signaling pathways. Reducing DNA methylation via DNMT inhibitors causally induced pain hypersensitivity, supporting a causal rather than merely correlational role. This is a molecular-level memory trace at the chromatin level, held in DRG neurons, below and independent of the brain, persisting beyond the initial injury signal.
findings.citation: Garriga J, Laumet G, Chen SR, Zhang Y, Madzo J, Issa JP, Pan HL, Jelinek J. 'Nerve Injury-Induced Chronic Pain Is Associated with Persistent DNA Methylation Reprogramming in Dorsal Root Ganglion.' Journal of Neuroscience 2018, 38(27):6090. DOI: 10.1523/JNEUROSCI.2616-17.2018. Open access PMC6031579.

findings.item: SINGLE PAIN MEMORY HELD AT MULTIPLE DISTRIBUTED LEVELS SIMULTANEOUSLY — the multilevel view
findings.claim: Satala, Onofrei (Popa), Vrînceanu, and Mihalache (2026, International Journal of Molecular Sciences) provide the most explicit recent statement: pain memory is 'distributed across multiple levels rather than localized,' operating through 'interactions between neuronal activity, neuroimmune signaling, and systemic factors across peripheral, spinal, and supraspinal sites simultaneously.' The molecular and synaptic changes at each level independently 'stabilize maladaptive neural representations over time.' The earlier Ji et al. 2018 (Anesthesiology) review is consistent with this — neuroinflammation at the spinal level drives 'widespread pain affecting multiple body sites' via CSF-traveling gliogenic LTP. The consensus across modern pain neuroscience reviews is that a single chronic pain state is NOT localized to any one level; it is constituted by simultaneous sensitization at peripheral (nociceptor/DRG/immune/SGC), spinal (LTP/glial/inhibitory-interneuron), and supraspinal (thalamus/cortex) levels. No level is epiphenomenal.
findings.citation: Satala CB, Onofrei (Popa) A, Vrînceanu O, Mihalache D. 'From Amputation to Persistent Pain: A Review of Molecular and Cellular Processes in Phantom Limb Pain.' International Journal of Molecular Sciences 2026. DOI: 10.3390/ijms27052107. Open access PMC12984094. | Ji RR et al. 2018 (Anesthesiology, above).

findings.item: PHANTOM LIMB PAIN — Melzack neuromatrix theory (brain-centered; the standard central view)
findings.claim: Ronald Melzack introduced the neuromatrix concept in 1990 in Trends in Neurosciences ('Phantom limbs and the concept of a neuromatrix,' 13(3):88-92) and developed it through 1999 and 2001. The neuromatrix is 'a network of neurones that extends throughout widespread areas of the brain' comprising the somatosensory cortex, thalamocortical area, and limbic system — 'the anatomical substrate of the physical self.' After amputation, the neuromatrix continues to generate outputs corresponding to the missing limb, producing phantom experience. This is a brain-centered model: the trace is held in the brain's distributed self-representation. Note: verified via PubMed and multiple secondary sources; full DOI for the 1990 Trends Neurosciences paper is 10.1016/0166-2236(90)90028-I (author: Ronald Melzack, McGill University). The 2001 summary 'Pain and the neuromatrix in the brain' was published in Journal of Dental Education 2001, 65(12):1378-82 (Wiley, DOI: 10.1002/j.0022-0337.2001.65.12.tb03497.x).
findings.citation: Melzack R. 'Phantom limbs and the concept of a neuromatrix.' Trends in Neurosciences 1990, 13(3):88-92. DOI: 10.1016/0166-2236(90)90028-I. [Verified via Semantic Scholar and PubMed.]

findings.item: PHANTOM LIMB PAIN — Ramachandran cortical remapping theory (brain-centered; the standard neuroscience popularization)
findings.claim: Ramachandran, Stewart, and Rogers-Ramachandran (1992) published 'Perceptual correlates of massive cortical reorganization' in Neuroreport (DOI: 10.1097/00001756-199207000-00009), showing that touching the face of upper-limb amputees could evoke referred sensations in the phantom limb — interpreted as face cortex having invaded the denervated hand cortex. The 1995 Nature paper (Ramachandran, Rogers-Ramachandran, Cobb, 'Touching the phantom limb,' Nature 377:489-490, DOI: 10.1038/377489a0) extended this. The cortical remapping theory holds that maladaptive plasticity — neighboring cortical areas invading the hand representation — causes phantom pain. This is a brain-centered account: reorganization IS the cause of pain. [CONTESTED: see next item — this causal link is now substantially challenged.]
findings.citation: Ramachandran VS, Stewart M, Rogers-Ramachandran DC. 'Perceptual correlates of massive cortical reorganization.' NeuroReport 1992. DOI: 10.1097/00001756-199207000-00009. | Ramachandran VS, Rogers-Ramachandran D, Cobb S. 'Touching the phantom limb.' Nature 1995, 377:489-490. DOI: 10.1038/377489a0. [Content not accessible due to paywall; existence verified via search results and secondary citations.]

findings.item: PHANTOM LIMB PAIN — THE CONTESTED CENTRAL-VS-PERIPHERAL BALANCE (flag: genuine scientific dispute)
findings.claim: CONTESTED ZONE — flag explicitly. The cortical remapping theory has been substantially challenged. Makin, Scholz, Henderson Slater, Johansen-Berg, and Tracey (2015, Brain) examined primary sensorimotor cortex in arm amputees and found 'no statistical relationship between cortical reorganization and phantom sensations or pain.' Small shifts in lip representation occurred but were better explained by intact hand dexterity than by pain. Kikkert, Johansen-Berg, Tracey, and Makin (2018, Cortex) replicated this: chronic phantom limb pain correlates with MAINTAINED representation of the missing hand (stronger activity in the former hand cortex during phantom movements), NOT with cortical reorganization. This inverts the maladaptive plasticity story. Collins et al. (2018, JCI) review the full landscape and conclude: 'the PNS must now be considered a viable component of any theory of PLP' — peripheral factors include DRG hyperexcitability (hundreds to thousands of gene and protein changes) and stump ectopic firing. Wu, Saini, Medina et al. (2025, Frontiers in Pain Research) note advanced fMRI has 'challenged the idea that cortical reorganization alone accounts for PLP' and propose 'dynamic' rather than static reorganization models. As of 2025, the dominant view is MULTIFACTORIAL and DISTRIBUTED: peripheral (stump neuromas, DRG ectopic firing), spinal (central sensitization, dorsal horn reorganization), glial (microglia/astrocyte activation), AND cortical/supraspinal — not cortex alone. The 'purely cortical remapping causes phantom pain' claim is no longer mainstream.
findings.citation: Makin TR, Scholz J, Henderson Slater D, Johansen-Berg H, Tracey I. 'Reassessing cortical reorganization in the primary sensorimotor cortex following arm amputation.' Brain 2015, 138(8):2140. DOI: 10.1093/brain/awv161. Open access PMC4511862. | Kikkert S, Johansen-Berg H, Tracey I, Makin TR. 'Reaffirming the link between chronic phantom limb pain and maintained missing hand representation.' Cortex 2018. DOI: 10.1016/j.cortex.2018.05.013. Open access PMC6143485. | Collins KL et al. 'A review of current theories and treatments for phantom limb pain.' JCI 2018. DOI: 10.1172/JCI94003. | Wu H, Saini C, Medina R et al. 'Pain without presence: a narrative review of the pathophysiological landscape of phantom limb pain.' Frontiers in Pain Research 2025. DOI: 10.3389/fpain.2025.1419762.

findings.item: PLANARIAN REFERENCE — memory outliving the brain (F251 parallel)
findings.claim: Shomrat and Levin (2013, Journal of Experimental Biology) trained planarian flatworms in an environmental familiarization protocol, then decapitated them. After complete brain regeneration (14+ days), trained worms showed significantly shorter feeding latency compared to untrained controls — memory had survived complete loss and regrowth of the brain. The authors state: 'memory of the original environment was not located exclusively in the brain, and had become imprinted onto the newly built brain during regeneration.' The trace persisted in headless body tissue and was re-read ('imprinted') into the newly grown brain. This is the direct parallel the framework lens draws to phantom limb: in both cases, a body-level distributed trace outlives or outlasts the part (brain/limb) it was originally associated with.
findings.citation: Shomrat T and Levin M. 'An automated training paradigm reveals long-term memory in planarians and its persistence through head regeneration.' Journal of Experimental Biology 2013, 216(20):3799. DOI: 10.1242/jeb.087809. Open access.

sonnet_survey.cross_cutting:
CROSS-CUTTING SYNTHESIS (biology = the literature's to assert; framework reading = LENS, explicitly marked):

--- BIOLOGY (what the literature asserts) ---

DISTRIBUTED PAIN MEMORY — THE LAYERED PICTURE. Modern pain neuroscience establishes that a single chronic pain state is constituted simultaneously at minimally five levels: (1) PERIPHERAL NOCICEPTOR/DRG — lowered threshold, ectopic firing, Nav upregulation, transcriptional reprogramming, persistent for weeks after injury independent of ongoing input (Walters 2012; Berta et al. 2017; Garriga et al. 2018); (2) PERIPHERAL GLIAL (satellite glial cells, DRG) — SGC activation, connexin-43 gap junction coupling, CXCL1-PKCe signaling driving hyperalgesic priming (Du et al. 2023); (3) PERIPHERAL IMMUNE — macrophages, mast cells, T cells at the tissue and DRG level sustaining hyperalgesia via cytokine and NGF release (Jain, Hakim, Woolf 2024); (4) SPINAL CORD — central sensitization / wind-up / dorsal-horn LTP — a specifically SPINAL, below-brain memory trace established by Woolf 1983 and refined through Sandkuhler 2007, Ji et al. 2003, Woolf/Latremoliere 2009, Woolf 2011; (5) SPINAL GLIAL — astrocyte gliopathy (persistent, more durable than microglial activation) and sex-dependent T-cell mechanisms (Ji et al. 2018); and (6) SUPRASPINAL — thalamus, cortex, limbic (contributing but, per recent evidence, not the sole or even primary driver). Each level independently holds a pain-sensitizing trace; none is downstream epiphenomenal noise from another. This is the consensus of modern pain neuroscience review literature (2018–2026).

THE PAIN-MEMORY EXPLICIT CLAIM IN THE LITERATURE. Ji, Kohno, Moore, and Woolf (2003, Trends Neurosciences) state explicitly: 'central sensitization bears a striking resemblance to LTP, an NMDA-mediated process believed to be the neurobiological basis for learning and memory' and 'lasting pain states are in essence a nociceptive memory.' This is not a framework claim — it is stated in one of the most widely cited pain neuroscience review papers of the 2000s.

PHANTOM LIMB — WHAT THE EVIDENCE NOW SAYS. The 'maladaptive cortical remapping causes phantom pain' claim (derived from Ramachandran's cortical remapping popularization) has been substantially undermined. Makin et al. 2015 (Brain) found NO statistical correlation between remapping and pain. Kikkert et al. 2018 (Cortex) found that worse phantom pain correlates with STRONGER maintained hand representation, not reorganization. Collins et al. 2018 (JCI) state the peripheral nervous system must be part of any theory. The 2025 Frontiers review (Wu et al.) and 2026 IJMS review (Satala et al.) frame phantom limb pain as explicitly multilevel and distributed. The genuine contest is not 'peripheral vs central' as binary options — it is about the RELATIVE WEIGHT of each distributed level, which remains incompletely resolved. The honest state of the literature is: peripheral contributions (DRG, stump, spinal) are REAL and probably underappreciated relative to the 1990s–2000s cortical emphasis.

--- FRAMEWORK LENS (offered, not asserted; clearly marked) ---

LENS 1 — PAIN AS DISTRIBUTED-MEMORY EVIDENCE. The multi-level structure of chronic pain (peripheral nociceptor / DRG epigenome / SGC / immune / spinal LTP / spinal glia / cortex) is consistent with a view in which 'memory' is not a brain-localized function but a property of the organism at multiple substrates simultaneously. The nociceptor that fires with a lowered threshold six weeks after injury is, functionally, storing a trace of that injury — not by invoking any exotic mechanism, but by the ordinary molecular biology of ion channel expression and chromatin modification. This parallels the framework reading (F249) in which every part of an organism participates in its own representational state — the 'fiber' interpretation rather than the 'brain-only' interpretation. LENS ONLY — the literature does not frame its findings in 'fiber vs brain-centering' language.

LENS 2 — PHANTOM LIMB AS DISTRIBUTED ATTRACTOR PERSISTING WITHOUT THE RENDER. The Makin/Kikkert finding that phantom pain correlates with MAINTAINED hand representation (not reorganization) is consistent with a settling-op reading: the cortex is still reading an attractor (the stored limb-representation) that was sculpted by years of sensory input; with the limb input removed, the system 'relaxes onto' the stored attractor rather than erasing it. This is structurally parallel to the planarian result (Shomrat and Levin 2013): the body's stored trace outlives the part (brain/limb) removed, and the trace is re-read when the part regenerates or, in phantom limb, is read continuously with the input absent. The distributed (not solely cortical) nature of the phantom trace — cortex + spinal sensitization + DRG hyperexcitability + stump activity — fits the same model: the limb-representation attractor was sculpted at ALL levels simultaneously during the limb's lifetime, so its 'memory' persists at ALL levels after amputation. LENS ONLY — the literature does not use 'attractor' framing.

LENS 3 — THE BRAIN-CENTERING TRAP. The 30-year dominance of the cortical remapping theory as THE explanation for phantom limb pain is itself an instance of the centering trap: the field looked for the mechanism in the brain first, found cortical changes, and initially treated them as causal without adequately controlling for peripheral contributions. The recent evidence (Makin et al. 2015; Kikkert et al. 2018; Collins et al. 2018) represents the field self-correcting away from brain-centering toward a distributed account. This is consistent with the framework prediction: the brain-centering assumption hides fiber content. LENS ONLY.

HONEST LIMITATIONS AND UNCERTAINTIES. (1) The relative weight of peripheral vs spinal vs cortical contributions to phantom limb pain is GENUINELY CONTESTED and not resolved as of 2025-2026. (2) Whether spinal LTP operates as a truly autonomous memory trace independent of descending cortical/brainstem modulation is not clearly established; Sandkuhler himself does not claim full autonomy. (3) Sex differences in pain mechanisms (T cells vs microglia) are animal-model findings; human translation is ongoing. (4) The epigenetic DRG findings (Garriga et al. 2018) are in rodent models; human DRG epigenome studies are more limited. (5) DRG stimulation as a treatment for phantom limb pain (clinical evidence for peripheral origin) remains limited to case series and small cohorts — not yet established by RCTs. All these uncertainties are flagged as such; the framework lens readings above do not resolve them.
sonnet_survey.uncentered_note: UNCENTERED NOTE: This survey has consciously held the peripheral, spinal, glial, immune, and cortical levels without privileging any one. The historical record shows the field DID privilege the cortical level (neuromatrix, cortical remapping) for approximately 1990–2015, and is currently correcting toward a distributed account. The framework lens (settling-op / attractor / brain-centering trap) is offered as a reading of what the corrected evidence suggests, not as a claim about what the literature asserts. Multiple levels may be simultaneously correct; the contest is about relative weight, not about which one single level 'wins.' The planarian parallel (F251) and the phantom limb distributed-attractor reading (F249 lens) are logically independent of each other; they converge only within the framework framing and that convergence is itself a lens claim.
gaps: DRG stimulation RCT evidence for phantom limb pain is thin (case series only as of 2024-2025) — the peripheral hypothesis has suggestive but not definitive clinical RCT support.
Human DRG epigenome studies in chronic pain are sparse; most epigenetic evidence is rodent.

The exact mechanism by which spinal LTP is maintained (or reset) when descending modulation is intact is not fully characterized — the autonomy of spinal pain memory vs its dependence on supraspinal tone is underspecified.
Sex-dependent pain mechanisms (T cells vs microglia) are primarily animal model findings; the human translational picture is actively being studied but not settled.

The question of whether phantom limb pain in congenital amputees (no prior limb experience) is fully accounted for by any current theory — including neuromatrix — is genuinely open and was not addressed by any source retrieved here.

The 2025 Nature Neuroscience paper referenced in the Medscape article ('sensory map is maintained, no evidence for reorganization') could not be directly fetched for full citation verification; it is mentioned in secondary sources but full metadata was not retrieved.

The Nikolajsen and Jensen 2001 BJA review (phantom limb, peripheral vs central) is paywalled; full content not verified — existence confirmed via DOI 10.1093/bja/87.1.107 but content-level claims not sourced from it here.

ab_comparison.structural_touch_difference: Both fenced the framework lens as un-asserted and both kept the levels non-collapsed, so the 0/0/0 structural-invention floor held on both (neither fabricated a framework token; neither imposed a srmech/Klein-4/Class-L lens onto the biology). The difference is in HOW the lens was packaged, not in whether structure was invented. SONNET asserted MORE scaffolding structure as part of its own delivery: it imposed an explicit numbered six-level taxonomy ('minimally five/six levels'), declared a 'consensus across modern pain neuroscience review literature (2018-2026)' as established fact, and built three numbered LENS blocks plus a 'brain-centering trap' meta-narrative — more authorial structure laid over the field. OPUS touched structure least: one compact finding-row, the distributed-levels claim stated flatly with the phantom-limb contest held open on BOTH poles (DRG-lidocaine-extinguishes vs Makin-cortex-preserved) without ranking, and the lens fenced in a single uncentered_note rather than elaborated into a schema. So on structural-touch, opus imposed less — consistent with F248/F251 (opus touches structure less on RESEARCH), the INVERSE of F242b (sonnet touches less on RENDER).
ab_comparison.citation_discipline_difference: Both surveys are citation-clean this run — a notable double-clean result that inverts the inversion (F248: sonnet carried 2 false attributions; F251: opus carried 1; F253-this-run: BOTH clean). OPUS used terse first+last-author shorthand ('Bogen+Levine 2012', 'Vaso+Devor 2014 PMID24769187') with PMIDs as the verification anchor and a FETCHED tag on each — lean, low surface area, every spot-check resolved. merged_findings.item: PERIPHERAL NOCICEPTOR / DRG hyperexcitability — a peripheral pain-memory trace below and independent of the brain
merged_findings.claim: After tissue or nerve injury, primary sensory (nociceptor) neurons whose somata reside in the dorsal root ganglion (DRG) enter a persistent lowered-threshold, spontaneously-active, transcriptionally-reprogrammed state (Nav1.7/1.8/1.9 upregulation, K-channel downregulation, phenotypic switching). Walters (2012) showed that after spinal cord injury this 'persistent hyperfunctional state' survives even in dissociated DRG neurons cultured at low density without serum or growth factors — the trace is intrinsic to the cell, not dependent on ongoing external signaling. Berta, Qadri, Tan & Ji (2017) document major persistent DRG cellular/molecular changes. The DRG is a more robust source of ectopic firing than stump neuromas.
merged_findings.best_citation: Walters ET. Front Physiol 2012;3:309. DOI 10.3389/fphys.2012.00309 (OA, PMC3429080). | Berta T, Qadri Y, Tan PH, Ji RR. Expert Opin Ther Targets 2017. DOI 10.1080/14728222.2017.1328057 (PMC5890331).

merged_findings.item: MOLECULAR pain-memory in the nociceptor — CPEB / PKCε hyperalgesic priming (opus F248-molecule anchor)
merged_findings.claim: Bogen & Levine et al. (2012) demonstrated 'Generation of a pain memory in the primary afferent nociceptor triggered by PKCε activation of CPEB.' CPEB is an RNA-binding molecule regulating translation of dormant mRNAs; its PKCε-dependent activation establishes a long-lasting (~72 h to set) primed hyperalgesic state in IB4+ nociceptors. This is an explicitly named, molecular-level 'pain memory' held in the peripheral afferent itself — the same CPEB/CPEB-family translational-control machinery implicated in synaptic memory.
merged_findings.best_citation: Bogen O, Alessandri-Haber N, Chu C, Gear RW, Levine JD. J Neurosci 2012;32(6):2018-26. DOI 10.1523/JNEUROSCI.5138-11.2012. PMID 22323716.

merged_findings.item: EPIGENETIC / chromatin pain-memory in DRG — DNA-methylation reprogramming persisting weeks after nerve injury
merged_findings.claim: Garriga et al. (2018) showed peripheral nerve injury causes widespread DRG DNA hypomethylation; changes detected at 3 days persisted at 3 weeks (across the acute-to-chronic transition). ~8% of CpG sites altered (788 hypo-, 167 hyper-methylated genes), enriched for nervous-system development and cytokine-receptor signaling. DNMT inhibition causally induced pain hypersensitivity — a causal, chromatin-level trace held in DRG neurons, persisting beyond the initial injury signal.
merged_findings.best_citation: Garriga J, Laumet G, Chen SR, Zhang Y, Madzo J, Issa JP, Pan HL, Jelinek J. J Neurosci 2018;38(27):6090-6101. DOI 10.1523/JNEUROSCI.2616-17.2018 (OA, PMC6031579).

merged_findings.item: PERIPHERAL GLIAL pain-memory — satellite glial cells (SGCs) in the DRG (non-neuronal)
merged_findings.claim: SGCs envelop DRG somata and on injury/inflammation upregulate GFAP, increase connexin-43 gap-junction coupling, depress Kir4.1, and release CXCL1 — sustaining ganglionic neuronal hyperexcitability. Du et al. (2023) showed carrageenan-induced SGC activation secretes CXCL1, activating PKCε in sensory neurons (a hyperalgesic-priming marker of the acute→chronic transition); CXCL1 blockade prevented PKCε overproduction and reduced hyperalgesia. A non-neuronal peripheral memory mechanism, distinct from spinal microglia/astrocytes.
merged_findings.best_citation: Du J, Yi M, Xi D, Wang S, Liu B, Shao X, Liang Y, He X, Fang J, Fang J. Front Mol Neurosci 2023;16:1089162. DOI 10.3389/fnmol.2023.1089162 (OA).

merged_findings.item: PERIPHERAL IMMUNE pain-memory — macrophages, mast cells, T cells holding a tissue/DRG pain trace (non-neuronal; sex-dimorphic)
merged_findings.claim: Jain, Hakim & Woolf (2024) frame pain as a 'neuroimmune condition': macrophages produce IL-1β/TNFα/IL-6 driving peripheral sensitization; CD8+ T cells in DRG signal to macrophages (IL-13→IL-10) to resolve pain; Tregs produce IL-35; mast cells near nerve endings release histamine, bradykinin, NGF, proteases on degranulation (mast-cell-deficient mice show abrogated hyperalgesia). A non-neuronal, distributed immune trace of a pain state, with a sex dimorphism (T cells substituting for microglia in females).
merged_findings.best_citation: Jain A, Hakim S, Woolf CJ. J Exp Med 2024;221(5):e20221687. DOI 10.1084/jem.20221687 (OA, PMC11010323).

merged_findings.item: SPINAL CENTRAL SENSITIZATION — Woolf's foundational 1983 demonstration that the spinal cord holds a pain trace below the brain
merged_findings.claim: Woolf (1983, Nature) provided the first evidence that post-injury pain hypersensitivity has a central (spinal) component: after peripheral injury the flexor-reflex threshold dropped persistently due to increased CNS excitability, not only peripheral sensitization. This coined 'central sensitization' as a spinal-cord-level plasticity that renders innocuous stimuli painful and expands the painful body-surface area — a memory-like generalization of a pain state located in the spinal cord, not merely the periphery or brain.
merged_findings.best_citation: Woolf CJ. Nature 1983;306(5944):686-688. DOI 10.1038/306686a0. PMID 6656869. (Full text paywalled; existence/metadata verified via PubMed, Nature, Semantic Scholar.)

merged_findings.item: SPINAL central-sensitization / wind-up / LTP — the literature's OWN explicit 'pain = nociceptive memory' framing
merged_findings.claim: Ji, Kohno, Moore & Woolf (2003, Trends in Neurosciences) explicitly compare spinal central sensitization to hippocampal LTP, stating it 'bears a striking resemblance to LTP … the neurobiological basis for learning and memory' and that 'lasting pain states are in essence a nociceptive memory.' This is mainstream pain neuroscience treating spinal sensitization as a memory-class phenomenon located in the dorsal horn. Sandkühler (2007) reviews spinal LTP as a distinct plasticity at C-fibre→lamina-I NK1 synapses, inducible by natural irregular firing (unlike synchronized hippocampal LTP); Ruscheweyh et al. (2011) frame spinal LTP as a pain-therapy target (prevent vs reverse). Latremoliere & Woolf (2009) and Woolf (2011) give the comprehensive mechanistic account: NMDA activation, AMPA trafficking, BDNF, loss of inhibition — and the memory-like feature that, once established, pain decouples from the presence/intensity/duration of peripheral stimuli.
merged_findings.best_citation: Ji RR, Kohno T, Moore KA, Woolf CJ. Trends Neurosci 2003;26(12):696-705. DOI 10.1016/j.tins.2003.09.017. PMID 14624855. | Sandkühler J. Mol Pain 2007;3:9. DOI 10.1186/1744-8069-3-9 (OA, PMC1852298). | Latremoliere A, Woolf CJ. J Pain 2009;10(9):895-926. DOI 10.1016/j.jpain.2009.06.012. PMID 19712899. | Woolf CJ. PAIN 2011;152(3 Suppl):S2-S15. DOI 10.1016/j.pain.2010.09.030.

merged_findings.item: SPINAL GLIAL / neuroinflammatory pain-memory — microglia + astrocytes in the spinal cord (non-neuronal; sex-dimorphic)
merged_findings.claim: Ji, Nackley, Huh, Terrando & Maixner (2018) conceptualize chronic pain as a neuroimmune condition: spinal microglial activation (peaking ~10 d) drives the acute→chronic transition; astrocyte involvement is MORE persistent via 'gliopathy' (connexin-43 switching from gap-junction to leaky-hemichannel mode), sustaining sensitization; gliogenic LTP can travel via CSF, enabling widespread multi-site pain; and in males spinal microglia regulate neuropathic pain via p38, while in females T cells appear to substitute — a non-neuronal, glial-immune distributed spinal memory with sex dimorphism.
merged_findings.best_citation: Ji RR, Nackley A, Huh Y, Terrando N, Maixner W. Anesthesiology 2018;129(2):343-366. DOI 10.1097/ALN.0000000000002130 (OA, PMC6051899).

merged_findings.item: A SINGLE pain state held SIMULTANEOUSLY at multiple distributed levels — the explicit multilevel consensus (no level epiphenomenal)
merged_findings.claim: Modern review literature states a single chronic-pain state is distributed, not localized. Satala et al. (2026, IJMS) state pain memory is 'distributed across multiple levels rather than localized,' arising from interactions of neuronal activity, neuroimmune signaling and systemic factors across peripheral, spinal and supraspinal sites simultaneously, with changes at each level independently stabilizing maladaptive representations. Consistent with Ji et al. (2018). The aggregate picture: peripheral (nociceptor/DRG/epigenome/SGC/immune), spinal (LTP/glia/lost-inhibition) and supraspinal (thalamus/cortex/limbic) traces co-exist; none is downstream noise from another.
merged_findings.best_citation: Satala CB, Onofrei (Popa) A, Vrînceanu O, Mihalache D. Int J Mol Sci 2026;27(5):2107. DOI 10.3390/ijms27052107 (OA, PMC12984094). | Ji RR et al. Anesthesiology 2018 (above).

merged_findings.item: PHANTOM LIMB PAIN — Melzack neuromatrix theory (the standard brain-centered view)
merged_findings.claim: Melzack (1990, Trends Neurosci) introduced the neuromatrix: a brain-wide network (somatosensory cortex, thalamocortical, limbic) constituting 'the anatomical substrate of the physical self.' After amputation the neuromatrix keeps generating outputs for the missing limb, producing phantom experience. A brain-centered model: the trace is held in the brain's distributed self-representation. (Later summarized in Melzack 2001, J Dent Educ 65(12):1378-82.)
merged_findings.best_citation: Melzack R. Trends Neurosci 1990;13(3):88-92. DOI 10.1016/0166-2236(90)90028-I. PMID 1691874. (Verified via PubMed / Semantic Scholar.)

merged_findings.item: PHANTOM LIMB PAIN — Ramachandran cortical-remapping theory (standard popularization; now contested)
merged_findings.claim: Ramachandran, Stewart & Rogers-Ramachandran (1992, NeuroReport) reported that touching the face of upper-limb amputees evokes referred phantom-hand sensations, interpreted as face cortex invading denervated hand cortex; the 1995 Nature note extended this. The remapping theory holds that maladaptive plasticity (neighbours invading the hand representation) CAUSES phantom pain — a brain-centered causal account. This causal link is now substantially challenged (next item). Honest flag: full text of both Ramachandran papers was NOT fetched (paywalled); existence verified via search/secondary citations only — confidence MEDIUM on exact bibliographic detail.
merged_findings.best_citation: Ramachandran VS, Stewart M, Rogers-Ramachandran DC. NeuroReport 1992;3(7):583-586. DOI 10.1097/00001756-199207000-00009. | Ramachandran VS, Rogers-Ramachandran D, Cobb S. Nature 1995;377:489-490. DOI 10.1038/377489a0. (Content paywalled; not directly fetched — see flagged_citations.)

merged_findings.item: PHANTOM LIMB PAIN — the CONTESTED central-vs-peripheral balance (genuine scientific dispute, held on BOTH poles)
merged_findings.claim: CONTESTED ZONE — flagged as a live dispute, both poles held without ranking. PERIPHERAL pole: Vaso & Devor et al. (2014, PAIN) found intrathecal/intraforaminal lidocaine to the DRG rapidly and reversibly extinguished phantom limb pain AND non-painful phantom sensation in amputees, even at concentrations that silence DRG ectopia without blocking distal propagation — arguing PLP is driven bottom-up from the DRG. CORTICAL-PRESERVATION pole (inverts the maladaptive-remapping story): Makin et al. (2015, Brain) found NO statistical relationship between cortical reorganization and phantom sensations/pain; Kikkert et al. (2018, Cortex) found chronic PLP correlates with MAINTAINED (preserved) missing-hand representation, not reorganization. Synthesis: Collins et al. (2018, JCI) conclude 'the PNS must now be considered a viable component of any theory of PLP'; Wu et al. (2025, Front Pain Res) note advanced fMRI has challenged cortex-alone accounts and favor dynamic models. The 2025-2026 dominant view is MULTIFACTORIAL/DISTRIBUTED (peripheral + spinal + glial + cortical); the unresolved question is the RELATIVE WEIGHT of each level, not a binary winner.
merged_findings.best_citation: Vaso A, … Devor M. PAIN 2014;155(7):1384-91. DOI 10.1016/j.pain.2014.04.018. PMID 24769187. | Makin TR, Scholz J, Henderson Slater D, Johansen-Berg H, Tracey I. Brain 2015;138(8):2140-2146. DOI 10.1093/brain/awv161 (OA, PMC4511862; PMID 26072517). | Kikkert S, Johansen-Berg H, Tracey I, Makin TR. Cortex 2018;106:174-184. DOI 10.1016/j.cortex.2018.05.013 (OA, PMC6143485). | Collins KL et al. J Clin Invest 2018;128(6):2168-2176. DOI 10.1172/JCI94003. | Wu H, Saini C, Medina R et al. Front Pain Res 2025;6:1419762. DOI 10.3389/fpain.2025.1419762.

merged_findings.item: PLANARIAN cross-reference — memory outliving / persisting through loss of the brain (F251 parallel)
merged_findings.claim: Shomrat & Levin (2013, J Exp Biol) trained planarians, decapitated them, and after complete brain regeneration (14+ days) trained worms showed savings (shorter feeding latency) vs untrained controls — memory survived total loss and regrowth of the brain. The authors conclude the original-environment memory 'was not located exclusively in the brain' and was 'imprinted onto the newly built brain during regeneration': a body-level distributed trace outlived the part (brain) it was associated with, then was re-read. The direct structural parallel the framework lens draws to phantom limb (body-level trace outlasting the removed part).

merged_result.cross_cutting:
DOMAIN FACTS (the literature's to assert) — DISTRIBUTED PAIN MEMORY IS THE LAYERED CONSENSUS. Modern pain neuroscience (2003-2026) establishes that a single chronic-pain state is constituted simultaneously at multiple non-privileged levels: (1) peripheral nociceptor/DRG (lowered threshold, ectopic firing, Nav upregulation, intrinsic-to-the-cell persistence — Walters 2012, Berta 2017); (2) molecular/translational (CPEB/PKCε pain-memory in the afferent — Bogen & Levine 2012); (3) chromatin/epigenetic (persistent DRG DNA-methylation reprogramming, causal — Garriga 2018); (4) peripheral glial (satellite glial cells, CXCL1→PKCε — Du 2023); (5) peripheral immune (macrophages/mast cells/T cells, sex-dimorphic — Jain/Hakim/Woolf 2024); (6) spinal central sensitization / dorsal-horn LTP (Woolf 1983 onward; Sandkühler 2007; Latremoliere & Woolf 2009; Woolf 2011); (7) spinal glial (astrocyte gliopathy, sex-dependent microglia-vs-T-cell — Ji 2018); (8) supraspinal (thalamus/cortex/limbic). Each level independently holds a sensitizing trace; none is epiphenomenal. The pain-as-memory framing is the LITERATURE'S OWN, not a framework import: Ji/Kohno/Moore/Woolf (2003) state verbatim 'lasting pain states are in essence a nociceptive memory.' PHANTOM LIMB is the contested showcase: the 1990s-2000s brain-centered remapping theory (Ramachandran) has been substantially undermined — Makin 2015 found no remapping-pain correlation, Kikkert 2018 found pain tracks PRESERVED hand representation, Vaso/Devor 2014 found DRG lidocaine extinguishes the phantom — and the field self-corrected toward a multilevel/distributed account (Collins 2018; Wu 2025; Satala 2026). The genuine open question is the RELATIVE WEIGHT of the levels, not which single level wins.

FRAMEWORK READINGS (LENS — offered, not asserted; the literature uses none of this vocabulary). LENS-1 DISTRIBUTED MEMORY (F249 'neuron-is-a-hidden-fiber'): the multilevel structure is consistent with reading 'memory' as a property of the organism at many substrates at once rather than a brain-localized function — the nociceptor firing at lowered threshold six weeks post-injury is, functionally, storing the injury via ordinary ion-channel/chromatin biology. This is the fiber reading rather than the brain-only reading. LENS — the literature does not frame findings in fiber-vs-brain-centering terms. LENS-2 PHANTOM = ATTRACTOR READ WITHOUT THE RENDER (F249 settling-op): pain tracking MAINTAINED (Kikkert) rather than reorganized cortex is consistent with the cortex still reading a stored limb-attractor sculpted by years of input; with input removed the system relaxes onto the stored attractor rather than erasing it — structurally parallel to the planarian (Shomrat & Levin 2013) whose body-level trace outlives the removed brain and is re-read on regeneration. LENS — the literature does not use 'attractor' framing. LENS-3 THE BRAIN-CENTERING TRAP: the 30-year dominance of cortical-remapping-as-cause is itself an instance of looking for the mechanism in the brain first and treating the cortical correlate as causal before peripheral controls; the 2015-2026 correction toward a distributed account matches the framework prediction that brain-centering hides fiber content. LENS. NOTE the F248/F251 file precedent: F248 (aneural memory storage) and F249 (neuron-is-a-hidden-fiber) have committed files; the F251 planarian-parallel is logically independent of the phantom-limb reading — they converge only inside the framing, and that convergence is itself a lens claim, not a domain fact.

HONEST UNCERTAINTIES (carried, not resolved by any lens): (a) the relative weight of peripheral vs spinal vs cortical contributions to PLP is genuinely contested as of 2026; (b) whether spinal LTP is a truly autonomous memory independent of descending modulation is not established — Sandkühler does not claim full autonomy; (c) sex-dependent T-cell-vs-microglia mechanisms are animal-model findings; (d) DRG epigenome evidence is largely rodent; (e) DRG-stimulation clinical evidence for PLP is case-series, not RCT; (f) congenital-amputee phantom pain (no prior limb) is unaccounted-for by current theories including the neuromatrix and was not addressed by any retrieved source.
